claims.text: The as-built Al0.2Co1.5CrFeNi1.5Ti0.3 alloy has a single-phase FCC matrix.
The as-built alloy has a uniform microstructure with minimal elemental segregation and grain-boundary oxidation.
The as-manufactured alloy has high ductility and toughness.
Oxidizing exposure at elevated temperature preferentially oxidizes Al and Ti at grain boundaries in this alloy.
Preferential oxidation produces continuous brittle Al-/Ti-rich oxide films or precipitates along grain boundaries.
Brittle grain-boundary phases concentrate stress and provide crack-initiation sites.
Grain-boundary oxide films weaken intergranular cohesion and promote intergranular cracking.
Intergranular cracking caused by grain-boundary oxidation can lead to rapid catastrophic failure under load.
High-energy grain boundaries accelerate oxidation reactions relative to the surrounding material.
Reducing atmospheres suppress oxide formation in this alloy and delay or alter its degradation pathway.
Diffusion-induced elemental segregation or phase instability may cause degradation even when oxidation is suppressed.
Samples exposed to an oxidizing atmosphere will develop more extensive grain-boundary oxidation than the as-built baseline and reducing- or inert-atmosphere samples.
Oxidizing exposure will decrease ductility and fracture toughness and increase brittleness relative to the as-built baseline.
Reducing or inert exposure will produce fewer or thinner oxide layers and better mechanical-property retention than oxidizing exposure.
The proposed comparison holds temperature and duration constant while varying the gas environment between ambient air and nitrogen or forming gas.
The proposed mechanism is applicable over approximately 600–800°C and exposure durations near 100 hours.
Outside the 600–800°C range, different degradation mechanisms may become active.
